instruction.text: Let’s listen in to find out the exciting news that has reached London! Fill in the gaps.

atoms.b: Shakespeare has been writing better than ever since he joined the Lord Chamberlain’s ((++Men Circus)).
atoms.sound: Shakespeare has been writing better than ever, since he joined the Lord Chamberlain’s men.

atoms.b: This weekend, their new project will finally be finished! The Globe Theatre will be opening its ((++doors presents)) to the public.
We must get our ((++tickets dresses))! It can hold 3,000 people and has an open-air stage. Do you know what’s showing?
Shakespeare has written a new ((++play song)) called Julius Caesar, which is set in Rome. It’s bound to be good!

feedback.end: In 1599, the Lord Chamberlain’s Men acting company built the Globe Theatre, which became the most iconic theatre in London and staged lots of Shakespeare’s greatest plays.

instruction.text: The Globe was open to all kinds of people. Select the different areas of the Globe to find out where they watched.

feedback.end: Sometimes, rich nobles paid to sit on the edge of the stage to show off their wealth.
It only cost one penny to stand and watch from the pit! The people who watched from here were known as groundlings.
It was more expensive to sit in the galleries, which were the first and second floors of the theatre surrounding the stage. This is where most wealthy people gathered.

atoms.b: The Globe had special features that made its performances more ((++entertaining dull)).
The roof above the ((++stage pitch)) was painted to look like a starry night and was known as “the heavens”.
Canon balls were sometimes rolled across the heavens to sound like ((++thunder sunshine)). They also created lightning flashes with firecrackers!

instruction.text: Select the trapdoor on stage to find out how it was used at the Globe Theatre.

feedback.finish: On stage, a trapdoor was used by actors to make sudden entrances, particularly when they were playing ghosts or evil spirits.

instruction.text: The special effects at the Globe could sometimes go wrong! Select the roof to find out what happened in 1613.

feedback.finish: In 1613, a canon was misfired and the thatched roof of the theatre set alight.

atoms.a: What do you think happened to the Globe after it burnt down?

feedback.end:
The Globe was rebuilt, but it was closed and pulled down around thirty years later.

A modern reconstruction of the theatre was opened in 1997 and now regularly shows Shakespeare’s plays!
